headline: New moon springs load up the rips as bonito push east toward the Shoals
subhead: Great Point and Monomoy are turning on with moving water while the first real bonito signal builds just west of us in Rhode Island Sound.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in early July — built toward a new moon and let the tide do the talking. We're coming into the springs now, and you could feel the current picking up all week at Great Point, at the Handkerchief, through the Monomoy rips. Wind sat mostly out of the southwest, nothing violent, just enough to push a light chop across Nantucket Sound and keep things from going glassy and dead. Water's held steady — not the abrupt jump you sometimes get this time of year, more of a slow creep warm, which is exactly the kind of thermal pattern that keeps bait comfortable and predators patient instead of scattering everything into a panic.

This week the moon goes new around the 11th-13th, which means big tidal swings — more water moving through the rips on both the flood and the ebb, shorter slacks, and a narrower window where the fish actually sit still. That matters a lot at Great Point and off Monomoy, where the whole game is reading when the rip stands up and when it goes soft. Bigger springs mean more bait getting swept off the shoals and more current seams for stripers and blues to sit in and let the food come to them. I'd rather fish moving water over a new moon than dead slack over a full — you get shorter windows, but the windows are better.

Striped bass have been steady, not spectacular, working the structure at Great Point on the last two hours of the ebb. Guys are doing well with umbrella rigs and bucktails tipped with sea worms worked slow along the seam where the rip meets the calmer water — that color change is the whole story out there, dirty green water butting up against the clean blue, and that's where the bass are stacking. Sizes have been mixed, schoolies mostly, but there've been slot fish mixed in for guys willing to grind through a tide change instead of leaving after twenty minutes. Monomoy's been fishing similarly — the rip off the Powder Hole and down toward the Handkerchief has held fish on the outgoing, particularly right at first light before the wind fills in.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player the last ten days. Schools have been working bait pods just off Sankaty and out toward the eastern edge of Nantucket Shoals, and when you find them they don't make you work for it — poppers and metal-lip swimmers get hit on the first cast most mornings. It's not the giant class of blues you sometimes see in the fall, more three- to five-pound choppers, but they're aggressive and they're consistent, which counts for something when the bass are being particular.

Fluke are where I'd point most boats right now. The pattern's been shifting out of the shallower Sound flats and into the channels and the deeper humps around Horseshoe Shoal and the edges of the Monomoy Channel — that's typical for mid-July once the shallow water starts running warm and the bigger fish slide toward cooler, deeper structure with better current flow. Squid strips on a bucktail-and-teaser combo, dragged slow along 25 to 40 feet of water on the last of the incoming, has been the most consistent producer. A few boats working the deeper cuts off Tuckernuck have reported keeper-class fish mixed with a lot of short ones, so it's worth covering ground rather than anchoring on the first fish you find.

Here's the one I'm watching closest. The cold wall that's usually held bonito penned up around Block Island collapsed on the Rhode Island side this past week, and the water out there jumped enough that bonito are spreading east across Rhode Island Sound instead of staying bottled up. That's not our water yet, but it's the signal I wait for every summer — when that eastern edge of the bonito range starts sliding, Nantucket Shoals is usually next, especially once the sand eels and peanut bunker start balling up along the rip lines off Great Point and the east side of the island. It's early. I wouldn't book a bonito trip off that alone. But it's the kind of development that tells me to start checking my epoxy jigs and small Deadly Dicks instead of leaving them in the bag until August.

No albies yet, and that's normal for the second week of July — that push usually doesn't show at Great Point until sand eels and peanut bunker start stacking up in numbers, typically late August into September on this side of the Cape. But the bonito signal moving our direction is worth logging now, because when they show, they show fast, and the guys who had gear rigged and ready are the ones who connect on day one instead of day five.

For the week ahead: I'd fish the new moon tide change hard at Great Point on the ebb, work the rip seam with bucktails and worked-slow swimmers for bass, and keep bluefish gear rigged for when you run into the blitzes off Sankaty — they've been easy to find lately. For fluke, work the deeper channels around Horseshoe Shoal and Monomoy on the incoming, squid strip and bucktail combo, and don't be afraid to move if the first drift is short-heavy. And keep half an eye east — if that Rhode Island Sound bonito push holds and the water out toward the Shoals keeps trending warm, this could be an early year for the first fish over the edge. I've seen it happen by the third week of July before. Doesn't mean it happens again, but that's exactly the kind of window I don't want to miss.
